CALIFORNIA TALENT AGENCIES ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Taylor Morgan

DECLARATION AND PURPOSE
This information sheet concerns the working relationship between Jordan Lee (the "artist") and Taylor Morgan, who is identified here as the artist's representative for entertainment-industry business matters, for reference only. This sheet summarizes provisions of California's Talent Agencies Act, Labor Code section 1700 et seq., which regulates who may lawfully engage in the occupation of procuring, offering, promising, or attempting to procure employment or engagements for an artist, requires that person or corporation to first obtain a license from the California Labor Commissioner, and gives the Labor Commissioner a role in hearing controversies arising under the Act.

This sheet is an informational record only. It does not determine whether Taylor Morgan's activities on behalf of Jordan Lee do or do not fall within the Act's definition of "talent agency," does not determine whether any particular engagement of Taylor Morgan by Jordan Lee is governed by the Act, and does not itself create, terminate, license, or otherwise affect any legal relationship between them. It is not legal advice and is not a substitute for reading the statute, and the case law construing it, directly.

WHO IS A "TALENT AGENCY": STATUTORY DEFINITION AND THE RECORDING-CONTRACT EXCEPTION
California's Talent Agencies Act defines who is regulated as a "talent agency." Labor Code section 1700.4(a) states: "'Talent agency' means a person or corporation who engages in the occupation of procuring, offering, promising, or attempting to procure employment or engagements for an artist or artists, except that the activities of procuring, offering, or promising to procure recording contracts for an artist or artists shall not of itself subject a person or corporation to regulation and licensing under this chapter. Talent agencies may, in addition, counsel or direct artists in the development of their professional careers."

Section 1700.4(b) defines "artists" broadly: "'Artists' means actors and actresses rendering services on the legitimate stage and in the production of motion pictures, radio artists, musical artists, musical organizations, directors of legitimate stage, motion picture and radio productions, musical directors, writers, cinematographers, composers, lyricists, arrangers, models, and other artists and persons rendering professional services in motion picture, theatrical, radio, television and other entertainment enterprises."

The statute's own text draws the regulatory line at the activity of procuring, offering, promising, or attempting to procure employment or engagements for an artist — not at a job title such as "agent" or "manager." It expressly carves the activity of procuring, offering, or promising to procure a recording contract, standing alone, out of what triggers licensure, and it expressly permits a talent agency to also counsel or direct an artist's career. Whether Taylor Morgan's specific activities on behalf of Jordan Lee do or do not fall within this definition is a determination this sheet does not make.

Talent agencies may, in addition, counsel or direct artists in the development of their professional careers."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1700.4(a), Labor Code § 1700.4(a) (definition of "talent agency") (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1700.4)

  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1700.4(b), Labor Code § 1700.4(b) (definition of "artists") (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1700.4)

This is one primary source checked twice for consistency, not two independent sources. This clause quotes subsections (a) and (b) of that same section; they are not independent of one another. Neither subsection states where the line falls between a person who occasionally helps arrange a single engagement and a person who is "engaged in the occupation" of procuring engagements — California case law addressing that line, and the related question of whether a "personal manager" can fall within this definition, is covered in a separate clause in this document rather than restated here.

LICENSING REQUIREMENT
The Act requires a license before anyone engages in the occupation of a talent agency. Labor Code section 1700.5 states: "No person shall engage in or carry on the occupation of a talent agency without first procuring a license therefor from the Labor Commissioner." The same section also requires that the license be posted in a conspicuous place in the licensee's office and that the license number be referred to in any advertisement soliciting talent for the agency.

This licensing requirement attaches to the occupation described in Labor Code section 1700.4 — procuring, offering, promising, or attempting to procure employment or engagements for an artist — rather than to any particular business title. Whether Taylor Morgan holds, or is required to hold, a license under this section is a fact this sheet does not state.

REQUIRED CONTRACT APPROVAL AND DISCLOSURE
The Act requires a licensed talent agency to use a form of contract approved in advance by the Labor Commissioner and to disclose its license status on the contract itself. Labor Code section 1700.23 states: "Every talent agency shall submit to the Labor Commissioner a form or forms of contract to be utilized by such talent agency in entering into written contracts with artists for the employment of the services of such talent agency by such artists, and secure the approval of the Labor Commissioner thereof. Such approval shall not be withheld as to any proposed form of contract unless such proposed form of contract is unfair, unjust and oppressive to the artist. Each such form of contract, except under the conditions specified in Section 1700.45, shall contain an agreement by the talent agency to refer any controversy between the artist and the talent agency relating to the terms of the contract to the Labor Commissioner for adjustment. There shall be printed on the face of the contract in prominent type the following: 'This talent agency is licensed by the Labor Commissioner of the State of California.'"

This sheet does not state whether any contract between Jordan Lee and Taylor Morgan has been submitted to or approved by the Labor Commissioner under this section, or whether it carries the disclosure language this section describes.

This clause relies on a single statutory section. Section 1700.23 itself cross-references an exception in Section 1700.45 (for contracts with a union-approved arbitration provision meeting stated criteria); that separate section has not been fetched or verified for this document, so this clause does not characterize it beyond noting that the exception exists.

LABOR COMMISSIONER'S ROLE IN CONTROVERSIES UNDER THE ACT
The Act channels disputes arising under it to the Labor Commissioner in the first instance. Labor Code section 1700.44(a) states: "In cases of controversy arising under this chapter, the parties involved shall refer the matters in dispute to the Labor Commissioner, who shall hear and determine the same, subject to an appeal within 10 days after determination, to the superior court where the same shall be heard de novo." The same subsection describes a bonding requirement to stay any money award pending appeal, and a procedure for the Labor Commissioner to certify, without a hearing, that no controversy exists when there is no dispute over the fee owed.

Section 1700.44(b) separately addresses what does not happen when a person fails to hold a required license: "Notwithstanding any other provision of law to the contrary, failure of any person to obtain a license from the Labor Commissioner pursuant to this chapter shall not be considered a criminal act under any law of this state." Section 1700.44(c) imposes a time limit: "No action or proceeding shall be brought pursuant to this chapter with respect to any violation which is alleged to have occurred more than one year prior to commencement of the action or proceeding."

This sheet does not state whether any dispute between Jordan Lee and Taylor Morgan is a "controversy arising under this chapter" for purposes of this section, and does not calculate any one-year period that might apply to a specific dispute.

CALIFORNIA CASE LAW: PERSONAL MANAGERS AND THE ACT
The California Supreme Court has addressed how the Act applies to a "personal manager" — a role the Act itself does not define — when that manager's activities include procuring employment. In Marathon Entertainment, Inc. v. Blasi (2008) 42 Cal.4th 974, the court observed: "The line dividing the functions of agents, who must be licensed, and of managers, who need not be, is often blurred and sometimes crossed." The court held that the Act's licensing requirement applies to a personal manager who procures employment for an artist, not only to someone who holds themselves out as an agent: "the strictures of the Talent Agencies Act (Lab. Code, § 1700 et seq.) (Act) apply to managers as well as agents."

The court also held that when a manager procures employment without a license, the Labor Commissioner is not required to void the entire management contract. The Labor Commissioner has authority to void the contract from its inception for that violation, but also has discretion, under the doctrine of severability, to enforce the lawful parts of the contract separately from the unlawful ones: "while the Labor Commissioner has the authority to void manager-talent contracts ab initio for unlawful procurement, she also has discretion to apply the doctrine of severability to partially enforce these contracts." This sheet does not state whether Taylor Morgan's activities on behalf of Jordan Lee involve procuring employment, and does not state how any severability analysis would apply to their arrangement.
